findings.title: All 14 success criteria trace to tasks — no gaps, no scope creep
findings.description: Every success criterion in `313-slice.world-bounds-policy.md` (Success Criteria §1–§14) maps to at least one task: SC1→1.1 (enum), SC2→1.2 (field + default), SC3/SC4→1.3+1.4 (loader validation, case-insensitivity, missing-key default, non-string and unknown-value errors), SC5→1.4 (`test_bounds_policy_yaml_round_trip`), SC6→2.3 OPEN tests + 3.4 mock test, SC7/SC8/SC9→2.2+2.3 (wrap half-open edge-exact, multi-width and negative overshoot, velocities unchanged, reflect clamp/flip including the inward-velocity idempotency nuance the slice's Policy Semantics section describes), SC10→3.2+3.4, SC11→3.4 (4 agents, outward velocities, 50 steps, per-policy assertions matching the half-open/closed rectangles), SC12→4.1/4.2, SC13→3.5+5.1, SC14→5.2 (walkthrough steps 1–8 mirror the slice's Verification Walkthrough 1:1, including the OPEN-drift regression guard). The deferred `SOFT` variant is correctly excluded from every task, honoring the slice's out-of-scope list — no creep. The scope-adjacent items that do appear (startup log line in 3.3, CHANGELOG in 5.4, status updates in 5.3) all trace to the slice's walkthrough step 4 and the task file's own Files-touched list plus project doc conventions. File anchors verified against the codebase: `WorldBoundsConfig` is indeed already imported in `simulation.py`, and the architecture doc line "(313) World Bounds Policy" exists at `project-documents/user/architecture/300-slices.worldserver-foundation.md:43` for Task 5.3's checkoff.

findings.title: Sequencing, test-with placement, and commit points are sound
findings.description: Dependencies flow correctly: enum (1.1) → field (1.2) → loader (1.3) → config tests (1.4); module skeleton (2.1) → helpers (2.2) → unit tests (2.3); constructor param (3.1) → step() call (3.2) → server wiring (3.3) → integration tests (3.4) → full-suite sweep (3.5). Test tasks immediately follow their implementation tasks (1.4 after 1.3, 2.3 after 2.1–2.2, 3.4 after 3.1–3.3). The one real sequencing hazard — Task 3.1 making `world_bounds` a required kwarg, which breaks every other direct `SimulationManager(...)` construction — is explicitly handled by Task 3.4 (call sites in `test_simulation.py`) and Task 3.5 (`test_force_builder.py`, `test_clients.py`, others), with the commit at 3.6 placed *after* the full suite runs in 3.5, so the commit point is green. All five commits (1.5, 2.4, 3.6, 4.3, 5.5) land at tested points: 1.5 after `test_config.py` passes, 2.4 after the new module's tests pass, 3.6 and 5.5 after full `pytest`, and 4.3 is safe because `tests/test_config.py:44-46` asserts only port on the real `default.yaml` (no policy assertion), so flipping it to `wrap` keeps the suite green. No circular dependencies; no per-task commit noise, no single end-commit either.

findings.title: Slightly granular task splits; Task 2.1 briefly references not-yet-defined helpers
findings.description: For a 2/5-effort slice, 15 tasks is on the fine-grained side. Two merges would tighten it without losing verifiability: Task 1.2 (add one dataclass field, one checkbox) folds naturally into 1.1 or 1.3, and Tasks 4.1/4.2 (each a one-line YAML edit to a different file with an identical verify command) could be a single "update shipped configs" task. Similarly, 2.1 and 2.2 both edit the same new file, and 2.1's `match` arms call `_apply_wrap`/`_apply_reflect` before they exist — this imports cleanly (names resolve only at call time) and the deferred test in 2.3 makes it safe, but a linter run at the 2.1 checkpoint would flag undefined names; merging 2.1+2.2 or stubbing the helpers would remove the wrinkle. None of this creates dependency or correctness risk — each task still has clear, junior-executable success criteria — so this is advisory, not blocking. Overall file count (one task file, 10 touched files) is proportionate to the slice.
